scenes.title: The idea: strings, indexes and f-strings
scenes.direction: Teach the index diagram, then the two ways to build text, then the form analogy and immutability. Quiz on indexes, then a breather.

visual.heading: A string is a row of characters
visual.label: The idea
body: Each character has a position, called its **index**. The first index is **0**.

segments.say: First, the idea. A string is a sequence of characters: letters, digits, spaces and symbols, in a row.
Each character has a position, called its index. And here is the surprise. The first index is 0, not 1.
You can also count from the end. Minus 1 is always the last character.

visual.heading: Two ways to build a message
visual.label: The idea
rows: Mixing text and numbers, and formatting them

segments.say: There are two ways to build a message from your variables.
You can join strings with a plus sign. That works well for a few pieces of text.
Or you can use an f string. It mixes text and numbers, and it can format them too.

visual.heading: An f-string is like a form
visual.label: Analogy
items: An `f` before the quotation mark makes an f-string.
Each `{ }` is a box that Python fills with a value.
Where it stops working: a box can also say **how** to show the value.
A string never changes. Methods give you a **new** string.

segments.say: An f string starts with the letter f, right before the opening quotation mark.
Think of it as a form with blank boxes. Each pair of curly brackets is a box, and Python fills it with a value.
The comparison stops at one point. A box can also say how to show the value, for example with two decimal places.
One more rule. A string can never be changed after it is made. You always make a new one.

visual.question: In the string `"CAFE"`, what is the index of the letter `F`?
visual.explain: Indexes start at 0: C is 0, A is 1, F is 2.

segments.say: Quick check. In the word cafe, in capitals, what is the index of the letter F?

after.say: B, 2. C is 0, A is 1, and F is 2. Counting from 0 takes practice, so keep this one in mind.

items: A string is a row of characters.
Indexes start at 0; minus 1 is the last.
An f-string fills `{ }` boxes with values.

visual.heading: Step 2: Build a message with an f-string

segments.say: Step 2. Asha stores her customer, a count and a price, as in Chapter 2.
Line 5 is an f string. The name inside the curly brackets is replaced with its value.

after.say: Line 5 says hello to Asha.

scenes.title: Step 3: Two decimal places
scenes.direction: Teach dot 2 f, then predict two lines, then reveal including rounding.

segments.say: Step 3. Line 4 prints the amount the plain way.
On line 5, after the name, there is a colon and a short code: dot 2 f. That is a format specification.
Dot 2 f means: a decimal number, with exactly two digits after the point.

after.say: Line 4 still shows 11.7. Line 5 shows 11.70. The format added the missing zero.
Line 6 shows the discount as 1.30.
And line 7 rounds ten divided by three to 3.33. The value itself never changes. Only the way it is shown.

scenes.title: Step 4: Columns
scenes.direction: Teach width, alignment and fill with a table, then the code, then the ask, then a quiz and a breather.

visual.heading: Step 4: Width and alignment
visual.label: Build it
rows: Centred, with `*` filling the empty space

segments.say: Step 4. To line up columns, the format can also set a width and an alignment.
A less than arrow and a number: the value takes at least that many characters, aligned left.
A greater than arrow aligns it right. That is perfect for prices.
A caret centres the value.
And a character before the arrow fills the empty space instead of spaces.
Line 4 prints a header. Inside the brackets, Asha writes text in single quotation marks.
Lines 5 and 6 use the same widths: 10 on the left for the name, and 8 on the right for the price, with dot 2 f.
Line 7 centres the word menu in 18 characters, and fills the space with stars.

ask.question: Lines 5 and 6: do the two prices line up? Why?

after.say: Yes. Every name takes 10 characters and every price takes 8, so both prices end in the same column.
And line 7 gives six stars, the word menu with a space on each side, and six more stars.

visual.question: Which code shows the price `6` as `6.00`, right-aligned in 8 characters?
visual.explain: `>` aligns right, `8` is the width and `.2f` gives two decimal places.

segments.say: Quick check. Which code shows the price 6 as 6.00, right aligned in 8 characters?

after.say: B. The arrow points right, 8 is the width, and dot 2 f gives two decimals.

items: An f-string mixes text and values.
`.2f` shows two decimal places.
Width and `<`, `>`, `^` line up columns.

scenes.title: Step 5: String methods

visual.heading: Step 5: Methods that clean text
visual.label: Build it
rows: The text without spaces at the start and the end
Each word with a capital first letter
All capitals, or all small letters

segments.say: Step 5. A method is a function that belongs to a value. You call it with a dot after the value.
Strip removes spaces at the start and the end.
Title gives each word a capital first letter.
Upper and lower change every letter to capitals, or to small letters.
And replace swaps one part of the text for another.

visual.heading: Step 5: Clean up a typed name

segments.say: A customer typed a name with extra spaces, and no capitals. Asha strips it on line 3.
Lines 5 to 7 try title, upper and replace.
Line 8 uses len. The len function counts every character in a string, spaces included.

ask.question: Line 8 prints two numbers. What are they?

after.say: Strip removed the spaces. Title, upper and replace each gave a new version.
And line 8 prints 13 and 9. The typed name still has 13 characters. Strip made a new string, and the old one never changed.

scenes.title: Step 6: Indexes
scenes.direction: Use the order code from Chapter 1. Predict four characters, then reveal.

visual.heading: Step 6: One character at a time

segments.say: Step 6. Remember the order code from Chapter 1? Asha stores it as a string.
To read one character, write its index in square brackets after the string. Use the rules from the idea section.

ask.question: Predict lines 3 to 6. Which characters do they print?

after.say: Index 0 is C, the first character.
Index 5 is the 1 right after the hyphen. Count from 0: C, A, F, E, hyphen, then 1.
Minus 1 is the last character, 4. And minus 2 is the T before it.
The code has 12 characters, so its indexes go from 0 to 11.

scenes.title: Work with AI: six stages, one receipt line
scenes.direction: The AI skill is a precise prompt. Then one conversation per stage on one receipt line. Stage 3 plants the missing f, stage 4 catches it, stage 6 catches .2.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: a precise prompt
visual.label: Before you start
items: Show the AI the **exact** output you want, character by character.
Compare the AI's result with your target, character by character.
No passwords or private data. Run every piece of AI code yourself.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill is a precise prompt.
When you want text in an exact shape, show the AI the exact output you want.
Then compare its result with your target, character by character.
And the safety habits still apply. No private data, and you run every piece of code yourself.

messages.text: I am a beginner learning f-strings. I want one receipt line: the name Sandwich on the left and the price 6.00 on the right, 24 characters in total. Do not write code yet. Which widths, alignments and format code do I need?

1. The name: width 16, aligned left with `<`.
2. The price: width 8, aligned right with `>`.
3. `.2f` shows the price with two decimal places.
16 + 8 = 24 characters in total.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha describes the exact line she wants, and asks for the widths and codes. No code yet.
The AI plans 16 characters on the left, 8 on the right, and dot 2 f. And 16 plus 8 is 24. That matches her target.

messages.text: I wrote the header row myself. Do not change it and do not run it. Predict the exact output, with a dot for every space.

Item...............Price
That is Item, 15 dots, then Price: 24 characters.
I counted 24 too. Then I ran it:

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha writes the header row herself. She asks the AI to predict it, with a dot for every space, so she can count.
The AI predicts the word item, 15 dots, then the word price.
Asha counts 24 characters too. She runs it, and it matches.

messages.text: Now write the line for one item: the name Sandwich and the price 6. Use the names item and price. Tell me exactly what it prints.
Here is the code. It prints `Sandwich            6.00`.
I ran it. This is what it printed:

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. Now the item line itself. Asha asks for the code, and asks exactly what it prints.
The AI gives a line, and promises Sandwich, spaces, then 6.00. It sounds sure.
Look at line 4 carefully. Remember how an f string starts.

ask.question: The AI says this prints `Sandwich            6.00`. Is it right?

after.say: Asha runs it. It prints the curly brackets and the codes, as plain text! And there is no error message to warn her.

messages.text: I expected `Sandwich            6.00`, but it printed the curly brackets as text. Compare the two and tell me the cause.
The `f` is missing before the opening quotation mark. Without it, the curly brackets are plain text. Add the `f`:

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha compares the real output with her target, and gives the AI both.
Now the AI names the cause. The f is missing, so the brackets are plain text. One letter fixes it.
Asha runs the fixed line. Sandwich, twelve spaces, 6.00. Exactly her target.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: My price came from a list of text, so I stored it with quotation marks. Now I get this error. First explain the cause and the line, then the smallest fix.

It is a `ValueError` on line 4. The format code `f` only works for numbers, but `price` is the string `"6"`.
The fix: store a number, `price = 6`, without quotation marks.

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Later, Asha copies a price from a list of text, so it has quotation marks. Python stops with a Value Error. She pastes the code and the full error.
She asks for the cause first. The AI explains that the f code only works for numbers, and the price is a string. The fix: remove the quotation marks.

messages.text: Review my receipt line. Suggest at most two improvements, each with one reason. Do not change what it prints.

1. Test it with a second item and a larger price, such as 12.5, to check that the columns line up.
2. Use `.2` instead of `.2f`. Both mean two decimal places, and `.2` is shorter.
Suggestion 2 would change the output. I tested it with two prices:

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. The line works. Asha asks for at most two improvements.
Suggestion 1 is good: test with a larger price. Suggestion 2 says dot 2 is the same as dot 2 f, only shorter.
Asha tests both codes with two prices. For 3.5, dot 2 looks fine. But for 12.5, it prints one point two, e plus zero one! Dot 2 means two digits in total. The AI was wrong again.
So Asha keeps suggestion 1 only. She tests a second item with a larger price, and keeps dot 2 f.
Both prices line up, with two decimals. Two AI mistakes caught, both by comparing the real output with the target.

visual.question: AI code prints `{price:.2f}` as plain text. What is missing?
options: The `f` before the opening quotation mark
visual.explain: Without the `f`, curly brackets are ordinary characters.

segments.say: Quick check. Some code prints the curly brackets and the format code as plain text. What is missing?

after.say: B. The f before the opening quotation mark.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistake 1 calls back to Chapter 2. Mistakes 2 and 3 are spot-it questions on rules taught earlier. Mistake 4 calls back to the debug stage.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: joining text and a number

segments.say: Mistake 1. Asha joins text and a number with a plus sign. The plus sign only joins strings to strings.
So Python stops with a Type Error, the same message you met in Chapter 2.
The fix is an f string. It turns the number into text for you.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: Now you try. The table code has two characters. Remember where indexes start.

ask.question: Line 3 works. What is wrong with line 4?

after.say: Index 2 does not exist. Two characters have the indexes 0 and 1 only, so Python reports an Index Error.
after.heading: Mistake 2: an index that is too large

after.say: The last index is always one less than the length. Or use minus 1 for the last character.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: spot this one too
visual.hidden_text: Find the mistake before the error appears.

segments.say: One more. Asha wants a capital A at the start of the name. Think about the rule for changing strings.

after.say: A string cannot be changed after it is made, not even one letter. Python says a string does not support item assignment.
after.heading: Mistake 3: changing one character

after.say: The fix: make a new string, for example with the title method, and give it the name.

visual.heading: Mistake 4: a decimal format for text

segments.say: Mistake 4 is the one Asha debugged with the AI. A price in quotation marks is a string.
Dot 2 f only works for numbers, so Python stops with a Value Error.
Store a number instead. In Chapter 4, you will learn to turn text into a number.

visual.heading: Read the last line first
visual.label: Common mistakes
rows: An index that is too large

segments.say: Here are all four, by the last line of the error.
Can only concatenate: a plus sign with text and a number.
Index out of range: an index that is too large.
Does not support item assignment: changing one character.
Unknown format code f: dot 2 f used on text.

visual.question: A string has 5 characters. What is its last index?
visual.explain: Indexes start at 0, so 5 characters have the indexes 0 to 4.

segments.say: Quick check. A string has 5 characters. What is its last index?

after.say: B, 4. Five characters have the indexes 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.

items: Use an f-string to mix text and numbers.
The last index is one less than the length.
Strings never change; make a new one.

segments.say: Let's recap.
A string is a row of characters. Indexes start at 0, and minus 1 is the last.
A plus sign joins strings. An f string puts values into text with curly brackets.
Dot 2 f shows two decimal places, and a number sets the width.
The arrows align left and right, and the caret centres.
Methods give you a new string. The original never changes.
And with AI: show the exact output you want, and test with more than one value.
